# Notifications

Turn on notifications, let each signed-in user register their browsers and phones and read their notification history, deliver to browsers with Web Push, and keep devices and history in Postgres or stores of your own.

## Turning them on

:::caution[In development]
Nothing sends notifications yet: sending, registering a browser, push on Android and iOS and the bell are coming soon.
:::

Notifications tell a user about something in the app, in a bell in the top bar and as push on their devices. You turn them on in `protobase.config.ts`:

```ts
import { defineConfig, notifications } from '@protobase/server'

export default defineConfig({
  extends: [notifications()],
  // config, auth, ...
})
```

Then run `protobase migration`, which writes the [devices and history tables](#table-names) as a migration of the project's own, and apply it with the project's migrations. `protobase dev` and `protobase serve` refuse to start while a table is missing or lacks what notifications need, and name it. Without `notifications()` there is none of it: no endpoints, no tables and no migration.

The bell and push are coming soon. `notifications({ ui: false })` keeps only the backend, without the bell.

## Devices

:::caution[In development]
A registered device receives nothing yet: sending is coming soon, and so are push on Android and iOS.
:::

A device is where a user receives push: a browser's push subscription, or an Android or iOS app's push token. Each signed-in user registers and removes only their own, through the API:

| Request | |
| --- | --- |
| `POST /api/notifications/devices` | registers the device the request comes from, or refreshes it; answers `{ id, kind, createdAt, lastSeenAt }` |
| `DELETE /api/notifications/devices/<id>` | removes the caller's device with that id; answers `204` whether or not the caller had it |

The body of a register is JSON (`Content-Type: application/json`, at most 8 KB), in one of three shapes:

```jsonc
// A browser: its PushSubscription as JSON
{ "kind": "web", "endpoint": "https://…", "keys": { "p256dh": "…", "auth": "…" }, "userAgent": "…" }
// An iOS app: its token in lowercase hex, the build's environment and bundle id
{ "kind": "apns", "token": "…", "environment": "production", "appId": "net.example.app" }
// An Android app: its token, and optionally its package name
{ "kind": "fcm", "token": "…", "appId": "net.example.app" }
```

A field that does not belong to the kind, a missing one, an unknown one such as a user id, or a value out of its format is a `400` that names the field and stores nothing. A browser's `endpoint` must be an https URL on one of the browsers' push services. `environment` is `sandbox` or `production`, and `userAgent`, optional for every kind, is at most 512 characters. The stored device keeps `null` in the fields its kind does not have.

Who may call them:

- Only someone signed in as themselves, with the token of their own sign-in. Visitors are refused with a `401`, and staff signed in as the user, outside apps acting for the user (such as an MCP client) and tokens minted with `issueToken` with a `403`.
- An app with its own `authenticate` marks a user's own sign-in on the session it returns, `signIn: { staff: false }`; without that mark, its sessions are refused.

A device is one token, or one endpoint for a browser. Registering a device someone else had moves it to the caller, as a new device with a new id that keeps nothing of the previous user's, so a shared phone or browser notifies whoever signed in on it last. A user keeps up to 20 devices: registering one more removes their least recently seen. Deleting a user removes their devices. <gap>Signing out cannot remove the session's devices because removing devices when a session ends is not implemented.</gap> Remove the device with `DELETE` before signing out.

The path comes from `devicesPath('/api', id)`, and the name of its id parameter from `deviceIdParam`, both exported by `@protobase/server`.

## History

:::caution[In development]
Nothing writes to the history until sending lands. <gap>The history cannot fill because sending notifications is not implemented.</gap>
:::

The history is each user's inbox: every notification sent to a user with the inbox flag on is kept for them, and one sent without it is only pushed. Sending, which fills it, is coming soon. Each signed-in user reaches only their own, through the API:

| Request | |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/notifications/history` | the caller's notifications, newest first: `{ items, next }` |
| `GET /api/notifications/history/unread` | how many are unread: `{ count }`, at most 100, so show `99+` from there |
| `POST /api/notifications/history/<id>/read` | marks the caller's notification with that id read; answers `204` whether or not the caller had it |
| `POST /api/notifications/history/read` | marks all read up to the newest one the caller was shown: `{ "upTo": "<its createdAt>" }`, then `204` |

Each item is `{ id, title, body, url, data, createdAt, readAt }`, with `readAt` `null` while unread. A notification read once keeps its first `readAt`, and marking all read leaves those read earlier as they were. Marking all read takes the `createdAt` of the newest notification the user saw, so one that arrives meanwhile stays unread.

The list gives 20 at a time, or as many as `?limit=` says, up to 50. A full page's `next` is a cursor: pass it as `?cursor=` for the page after it, until `next` is `null`. A limit or cursor out of its format, and a parameter or body field the request does not take, such as a user, is a `400` that changes nothing. Both marks take JSON (`Content-Type: application/json`): marking one takes an empty body or `{}`. Answers about the history are never cached.

`title` and `body` are plain text: show them as text, never as HTML. `url` is a path on the app, such as `/tasks/42`, or an absolute URL on one of the app's own origins; anything else, another site, `javascript:` or `data:`, is answered as `null`. A notification's `url` and `data` are kept until its user is removed, so leave one-time links and secrets out of inbox notifications.

The same people may call them as may [register devices](#devices): only someone signed in as themselves. With Protobase's auth, deleting a user removes their history; an app that deletes users otherwise calls `historyStore(db, options).removeAllForUser(userId)` as it deletes one, with the options it gave `notifications()`.

The paths come from `historyPath('/api')`, `historyPath('/api', 'unread')`, `historyPath('/api', 'read')` and `historyPath('/api', { read: id })`, and the name of the id parameter from `historyIdParam`, all exported by `@protobase/server`.

## Web Push

:::caution[In development]
Browsers cannot register for push yet, so nothing reaches them until browser registration lands.
:::

Browsers receive push through the Web Push protocol: desktop and Android browsers, and web apps added to the home screen on iPhone. You generate a key pair with the CLI and set it, with a contact address, in three environment variables:

```sh
protobase notifications vapid-keys
```

| Variable | |
| --- | --- |
| `PROTOBASE_VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY` | the public key the command prints |
| `PROTOBASE_VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY` | the private key the command prints |
| `PROTOBASE_VAPID_SUBJECT` | how push services reach you: a `mailto:` address or an `https:` URL |

Without them Web Push is off and the app has no sender for browsers. One or two of them set, a blank one, a key that is not one, or a public key that is not the private key's stops startup, naming the variable without its value.

The private key is a secret: keep it out of client code, `VITE_` variables and the repository. Anyone holding it and the stored subscriptions can push to every subscribed browser. Browsers subscribe with the public key, which `/meta` gives every caller as `notifications.webPushKey`, so a new key pair breaks every subscription until its browser registers again.

Each message is encrypted for its browser and signed with the key. It goes only to an endpoint on one of the browsers' push services, never through a redirect; a device stored with any other endpoint, or with keys that are not a subscription's, is `refused`. <gap>Web Push cannot deliver to a push service outside the browsers' own because adding one to the list is not implemented.</gap> A message's `platform.web` sets the request's `ttl`, `urgency` and `topic` and fields merged into the JSON the browser receives (`payload`), in place of those built from the message; every URL in that JSON is checked as the message's `url` is. The JSON carries at most 3993 bytes.

## Your own parts

:::caution[In development]
The device store, the history store and the senders can be replaced; the bell is coming soon.
:::

The device store is an interface with a Postgres default, the [devices table](#table-names). You pass your own store to `notifications()`, such as one from a package that keeps devices elsewhere, and then no table is needed and `protobase migration` writes none:

```ts
import { defineConfig, notifications, type DeviceStore } from '@protobase/server'

const store: DeviceStore = {
  register: async (userId, device) => { /* add, refresh, or move the token to userId as a new device */ },
  remove: async (userId, id) => { /* only when the device is userId's */ },
  listForUser: async (userId) => [],
  listByIds: async (ids) => [],
  removeGone: async (tokens) => {},
  removeAllForUser: async (userId) => {},
}

export default defineConfig({ extends: [notifications({ store })] })
```

Every method takes and returns plain data: the user id as text, and devices as `{ id, userId, kind, token, p256dh, auth, environment, appId, userAgent, createdAt, lastSeenAt }`, with `token` the endpoint for a browser. A method given an empty user id, id or token throws. `listByIds` and `removeGone` act on any user's devices, for the code that sends; the endpoints never call them. A store missing a method stops startup, naming it.

When Protobase's auth deletes a user, by an admin or with `protobase users delete`, it calls the store's `removeAllForUser` before anything is deleted, so a store that throws stops the deletion, and once more afterwards. An app that deletes users otherwise calls `deviceStore(db, options).removeAllForUser(userId)` as it deletes one, with the options it gave `notifications()`.

The history store is an interface with a Postgres default too, the [history table](#table-names), and you pass your own as `historyStore`:

```ts
import { defineConfig, notifications, type HistoryStore } from '@protobase/server'

const historyStore: HistoryStore = {
  record: async (userId, notification) => { /* keep it unread, created now, under a new id */ },
  list: async (userId, { before, limit }) => [], // newest first, after `before`
  countUnread: async (userId) => 0, // counting up to 100
  markRead: async (userId, id) => false, // true when userId has it
  markAllRead: async (userId, upTo) => {}, // the unread ones created up to `upTo`
  removeAllForUser: async (userId) => {},
}

export default defineConfig({ extends: [notifications({ historyStore })] })
```

A notification is `{ id, userId, title, body, url, data, createdAt, readAt }`, and `before` is the `{ createdAt, id }` of the last one of the page before. Each method touches only the given user's notifications, and throws on an empty user id or id. An id is letters, digits, `-` and `_`, at most 64 characters, as it goes into a path. `record` keeps only what `historyLimits` allows: a title of up to 256 characters, a body and a url of up to 2048, and `data` of up to 4096 bytes of JSON. The endpoints answer with an error, showing nothing of it, when a store gives back another user's notification. A store missing a method stops startup, naming it. Deleting a user calls its `removeAllForUser` as it does the device store's; an app that deletes users otherwise calls `historyStore(db, options).removeAllForUser(userId)`.

### Senders

A sender delivers notifications to the devices of the kinds it names, through their push service. Web Push is built in; you pass your own senders to `notifications()`, such as from a package, and they replace the built-in ones, at most one for each kind:

```ts
import { defineConfig, notifications, type PushSender } from '@protobase/server'

const sender: PushSender = {
  kinds: ['fcm'],
  send: async (message, devices) => devices.map((device) => ({ id: device.id, result: 'ok' })),
}

export default defineConfig({ extends: [notifications({ senders: [sender] })] })
```

`send` takes a message and a batch of devices of those kinds, and answers each device by its id with a result:

| Result | |
| --- | --- |
| `ok` | the push service took the message |
| `gone` | the device no longer exists there, and should be removed |
| `retry` | the push service may take it later; `retryAfterSeconds` says when, if the service does |
| `refused` | the sender never delivers to the device as it is stored, so it is neither retried nor removed |

A device with no answer, or an answer that is none of these, counts as `retry`, and answers for devices outside the batch are ignored. What a sender throws becomes an error that names only the sender's place in the list, since its own error may name devices.

A message is plain data:

| Field | |
| --- | --- |
| `title` | the title, required |
| `body` | the text under it |
| `url` | opened on tap: an absolute `http` or `https` URL, on the app's origin or any other |
| `data` | JSON the app reads when the notification is opened |
| `badge` | the number on the app's icon |
| `sound` | the sound to play |
| `tag` | a later notification with the same tag replaces this one: up to 32 letters, digits, `-` and `_` |
| `ttl` | how long, in seconds, a push service keeps it for a device that is offline, up to 28 days |
| `urgency` | `very-low`, `low`, `normal` or `high` |
| `platform` | each protocol's own fields: `web`, `apns` and `fcm` |

`pushMessage(message)` checks a message and answers it as senders get it, or throws a `PushMessageError` that names the field at fault, never its value. Every sender gets a checked message: a `url` with any other scheme, such as `javascript:` or `data:`, or a relative one, is refused, and so is a field that is not one of the message's, a key `__proto__`, `constructor` or `prototype` anywhere in it, or text with control characters. A sender for `web` devices names the VAPID `publicKey` browsers subscribe with, which `/meta` gives every caller; it must be a P-256 public key in base64url.

The bell is coming soon.

## Table names

:::caution[Beta]
Both tables are written and checked; nothing writes to the history table until sending lands.
:::

The default store keeps devices in the table `devices` of the schema `notifications`:

| Column | |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | `uuid`, the id the endpoints answer with |
| `user_id` | the user's id, of the same type as auth's users table's `id`; with Protobase's auth a foreign key to that table, so a deleted user's devices go with them |
| `kind` | `web`, `apns` or `fcm` |
| `token` | the token, or a browser's endpoint; unique |
| `p256dh`, `auth` | a browser's keys |
| `environment` | an iOS app's `sandbox` or `production` |
| `app_id` | the app's bundle id or package name |
| `user_agent` | what the device said it is |
| `created_at`, `last_seen_at` | when the user registered it, and last refreshed it |

You rename the schema, the table and each column, as auth takes `users.table` and `users.columns`, such as to keep devices in a table you already have:

```ts
notifications({
  schema: 'push',
  devices: { table: 'targets', columns: { user_id: 'owner_id', token: 'address' } },
})
```

The history is kept in the table `history` of the same schema:

| Column | |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | `uuid`, the id the endpoints answer with |
| `user_id` | the user's id, as in the devices table; with Protobase's auth a foreign key to auth's users table, so a deleted user's history goes with them |
| `title`, `body` | the text it shows |
| `url` | where it leads |
| `data` | `jsonb`, the app's own |
| `created_at` | when it was kept |
| `read_at` | when its user read it, `NULL` while unread |

Two indexes keep a user's newest-first pages and unread count cheap. You rename its table and columns as `history.table` and `history.columns`:

```ts
notifications({
  history: { table: 'inbox', columns: { user_id: 'owner_id', read_at: 'seen_at' } },
})
```

A name is lowercase letters, digits and `_`, at most 63 characters. Startup stops, naming what is wrong, while a table lacks a configured column, while the devices table lacks a unique index on the token column alone, which moving a device relies on, or, with Protobase's auth, while either table lacks the foreign key from its user column to the users table with `on delete cascade`.
